# Knitting runs from the note's own folder, but the results live under the
# project root. Walk up to the folder holding the .Rproj rather than hardcoding
# "..", so the note keeps working wherever it is moved inside the project.
find_root <- function(dir = normalizePath(getwd())) {
  repeat {
    if (length(list.files(dir, pattern = "\\.Rproj$"))) return(dir)
    parent <- dirname(dir)
    if (parent == dir)
      stop("No .Rproj found above ", getwd(), "; cannot locate the project root.")
    dir <- parent
  }
}

```{r rates}
# The rates, recomputed here exactly as Section 2 of the script does, so this
# note is self-contained.
raw <- read_csv(DATA, show_col_types = FALSE)
obs <- raw %>% filter(method == "obs") %>%
  mutate(pair = paste(higher_level, lower_level, sep = "||"))
cam <- raw %>% filter(method == "rpi") %>%
  transmute(higher_level, lower_level, focal_site, camera = ground_truth)

tp <- sum(obs$ground_truth == 1 & obs$prediction == 1)
fp <- sum(obs$ground_truth == 0 & obs$prediction == 1)
fn <- sum(obs$ground_truth == 1 & obs$prediction == 0)
tn <- sum(obs$ground_truth == 0 & obs$prediction == 0)
EPS_Y <- 1 - (tp / (tp + fn) + tn / (tn + fp)) / 2

both   <- obs %>% inner_join(cam, by = c("higher_level", "lower_level",
                                         "focal_site"))
TPc    <- sum(both$ground_truth == 1 & both$camera == 1)
A_only <- sum(both$ground_truth == 1 & both$camera == 0)
B_only <- sum(both$ground_truth == 0 & both$camera == 1)
EPS_L  <- 1 - TPc / (TPc + B_only)
JACC   <- TPc / (TPc + A_only + B_only)
F_POS  <- 0.05

# p1 and nu: zero-truncated beta-binomial, the same likelihood as the script
# every site is a trial for every pair, as in the script (Section 1 and 2)
N_SITES <- n_distinct(obs$focal_site)
pairs_tbl <- obs %>% group_by(pair) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(ground_truth), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(R = N_SITES) %>%
  filter(n >= 1)
nll <- function(par) {
  m <- plogis(par[1]); nu <- exp(par[2])
  a <- m * nu; b <- (1 - m) * nu
  lp <- function(k, N) lbeta(k + a, N - k + b) - lbeta(a, b)
  -sum(lp(pairs_tbl$n, pairs_tbl$R) - log1p(-exp(lp(0, pairs_tbl$R))))
}
fit <- optim(c(0, log(5)), nll)
P1 <- plogis(fit$par[1]); NU <- exp(fit$par[2]); LL_BB <- -fit$value

# the same likelihood with nu removed: one shared p1, refitted
nll_hom <- function(par) {
  p  <- plogis(par)
  lp <- function(k, N) k * log(p) + (N - k) * log1p(-p)
  -sum(lp(pairs_tbl$n, pairs_tbl$R) - log1p(-exp(lp(0, pairs_tbl$R))))
}
hom <- optimize(nll_hom, c(-8, 8))
P1_HOM <- plogis(hom$minimum); LL_B <- -hom$objective
LR_NU  <- 2 * (LL_BB - LL_B)
P_NU   <- 0.5 * pchisq(LR_NU, 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
NPAIRS <- nrow(pairs_tbl)

KAPPA <- (1 - EPS_Y) * (1 - F_POS) / ((1 - F_POS) + EPS_L)
N_CLIP <- sum(obs$probability == 0.5)

one   <- post %>% filter(run == "A-uniform")
N_PF  <- sum(one$det_category == "possibly forbidden")
```

is_supported <- grepl(sprintf("^supported in %d/%d$", length(RUNS), length(RUNS)),
                      camsum$verdict)
N_SUPPORTED <- sum(is_supported)
# only among the supported: a contradicted category can "hold" too, in the
# wrong direction, and must not be counted here
N_SUPPORTED_SITE <- sum(is_supported & camsum$site %in% "holds")
```

> Every candidate link at Cabrera carries eight posterior probabilities, one per
> link category, instead of a single hard label. `r N_SUPPORTED` of the eight
> categories behave the way they claim to when tested against camera records the
> posterior never saw. Replication saturates within the six-site design, so what
> uncertainty remains is not something more sites can fix.

               "Prior and model settings compared",
               "Categories confirmed against cameras in all four settings",
               "Ceiling on confidence for a link not seen locally"),
  Value = c(format(nrow(one), big.mark = ","),
            sprintf("%d (%.0f%%)", sum(!is.na(one$camera)),
                    100 * mean(!is.na(one$camera))),
            as.character(sum(one$camera == 1, na.rm = TRUE)),
            as.character(length(RUNS)),

) %>% show()
```

# Overview

## Motivation

The framework sorts every candidate link into one of eight categories using
three yes/no facts: does the model predict it, was it seen at this site, was it
seen at another site in the same system. Three bits, eight boxes.

The weakness is that the answer is a **label**. A link that only just qualified
looks identical to one that clearly belongs, and the label says nothing about
which links to chase or what would settle the question.

The posterior replaces the label with a probability spread across all eight
categories. It says how much of a link's evidence really supports its assigned
category, which alternative the doubt points toward, and what the cheapest way
to raise confidence would be.

## What the pipeline does

1. **Estimates the error rates** from the data itself.
2. **Calibrates the raw model scores** so they read as probabilities, and checks
   that the hard categorisation is unchanged.
3. **Builds one posterior function** holding every ingredient from the SI.
4. **Checks that function against the SI's published worked values.**
5. **Runs it under four settings** of prior and model handling.
6. **Produces** category maps, category distributions, a test against camera
   records, and an evidence-accumulation curve.

::: {.method}
**Methodological decisions.** The posterior is one function, and each setting
below is an argument to it rather than a separate implementation, so the
equation in the manuscript and the code cannot drift apart. Calibration is Platt
scaling fitted **site-blocked**, so no site calibrates itself. Platt is monotone
and therefore cannot reorder links, which we verify rather than assert: the hard
predictions survive intact and only the number on the threshold moves.
:::

## The posterior

Each candidate link $i$ carries four pieces of evidence $E_i$:

- $\hat Y_i \in \{0,1\}$, whether the model predicts it
- $O_{l,i} \in \{0,1\}$, whether it was recorded at the focal site
- $R$, the number of replicates, which is every site except the focal one, the
  same for every link
- $n_i \le R$, how many of those replicates recorded the interaction

Each category is one combination of three **true** states, which the evidence
reports with error: $z_Y$, an error-free model would predict it; $z_l$, it is
realised at the focal site; $z_r$, it is realisable in the replicates.

| Category | $z_Y$ | $z_l$ | $z_r$ |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| recurrent | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| locally unique | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| possibly missing | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| phantom | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| model-elusive | 0 | 1 | 1 |
| weakly-supported | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| locally absent | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| possibly forbidden | 0 | 0 | 0 |

The probability that link $i$ belongs to category $k$ is the prior times three
likelihood factors, rescaled so the eight probabilities sum to one:

$$
P(k \mid E_i) \;=\; \frac{\pi(k)\; L_Y(k)^{\,s}\; L_l(k)\; L_r(k)}
{\sum_{k'} \pi(k')\; L_Y(k')^{\,s}\; L_l(k')\; L_r(k')}
$$

$s$ switches the model factor on ($s = 1$) or off ($s = 0$); the settings below
say when.

**Model factor.** The model agrees with the true state at rate $1-\epsilon_Y$:

$$
L_Y = \begin{cases} 1-\epsilon_Y & \text{if } \hat Y = z_Y \\ \epsilon_Y & \text{if } \hat Y \neq z_Y \end{cases}
$$

**Local factor.** A realised link is missed at rate $\epsilon_l$; an unrealised
one is recorded spuriously at rate $f$:

$$
L_l = \begin{cases}
1-\epsilon_l \text{ if } O_l = 1, \quad \epsilon_l \text{ if } O_l = 0 & \text{when } z_l = 1 \\
f \text{ if } O_l = 1, \quad 1-f \text{ if } O_l = 0 & \text{when } z_l = 0
\end{cases}
$$

**Replicate factor.** The chance of $n$ detections in $R$ sites. A realisable
link is detected at a rate that varies between links, with mean $p_1$ and
concentration $\nu$ (a beta-binomial). A non-realisable link is detected only by
mistake, at rate $f$ (a binomial):

$$
L_r = \begin{cases}
\dfrac{B(n+a,\; R-n+b)}{B(a,\,b)}, \quad a = p_1\nu,\; b = (1-p_1)\nu & \text{when } z_r = 1 \\[2ex]
f^{\,n}\,(1-f)^{R-n} & \text{when } z_r = 0
\end{cases}
$$

$B$ is the beta function. The binomial coefficient is left out because it is the
same for every category and cancels.

::: {.method}
**Methodological decision: every other site is a replicate.** A link can go
unrecorded at a replicate because the partners were not there, or because they
were there and the interaction was not realised or not detected. The SI does not
separate these: both sit inside the per-replicate rate
$p_1 = \rho\,(1-\epsilon_l)$, where the realisation rate $\rho$ is the whole
ecological step, co-occurrence included (SI Section S4, Table S7). So $R$ counts
every other site for every link, including sites where the two partners were
never recorded together.

There is also an ecological reason not to drop those sites. A species enters a
site's data only if it was recorded interacting there, and co-occurring species
are not always detected. A site without both partners in its data may well have
held both, so excluding it would treat an undetected species as an absent one.
:::

**Prior.** One probability per true state, multiplied:

$$
\pi(k) = \pi_Y^{\,z_Y}(1-\pi_Y)^{1-z_Y}\;\; \pi_l^{\,z_l}(1-\pi_l)^{1-z_l}\;\; \pi_r^{\,z_r}(1-\pi_r)^{1-z_r}
$$

Setting all three to $\tfrac12$ gives every category $\tfrac18$, the uniform
prior.

## The rates

```{r rate-table}
tibble(
  Rate = c("$\\epsilon_Y$", "$\\epsilon_l$", "$f$", "$p_1$", "$\\nu$"),
  Meaning = c("model error, 1 - balanced accuracy",
              "chance direct observation misses a link that is present",
              "chance a record is spurious",
              "chance a replicate site records a link that is present",
              "how variable that chance is between links"),
  Value = c(sprintf("%.3f", EPS_Y), sprintf("%.3f", EPS_L),
            sprintf("%.2f", F_POS), sprintf("%.3f", P1), sprintf("%.2f", NU))
) %>% show()
```

::: {.method}
**Methodological decisions.**

$\epsilon_Y$ is one minus the balanced accuracy of the leave-one-site-out
predictions against direct observation, one rate for both directions of error:

$$
\epsilon_Y = 1 - \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{TP}{TP+FN} + \frac{TN}{TN+FP}\right)
$$

$\epsilon_l$ comes from the camera contrast: both methods watch the same site at
the same time, so the difference between them is detection alone. Over the pairs
both methods had in play, with $O$ the links recorded by direct observation and
$C$ those recorded by camera:

$$
\epsilon_l = 1 - \frac{|O \cap C|}{|C|}
$$

Conditioning on the links the **cameras** recorded makes the estimate
directional, as "chance of missing something present" requires.

This is the **Lincoln-Petersen two-sample estimator**, the classic
capture-recapture method. Two independent surveys of the same population give an
estimate of the population's total size:

$$
\hat N = \frac{|O| \; |C|}{|O \cap C|}
$$

Here the population is the interactions present, the first survey is direct
observation and the second is the cameras. The share of that population direct
observation records is $|O| / \hat N$, and substituting $\hat N$ gives exactly
the expression above:

$$
\frac{|O|}{\hat N} = \frac{|O \cap C|}{|C|}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\epsilon_l = 1 - \frac{|O|}{\hat N} = 1 - \frac{|O \cap C|}{|C|}
$$

The estimate is unbiased when the two methods miss links independently. Where
both tend to miss the same hard links, it understates $\epsilon_l$.

A symmetric alternative gives the wrong answer: $1 -$ Jaccard would be
`r sprintf("%.2f", 1 - JACC)`, because it also charges direct observation for
links the *cameras* missed.

$f$ is the one rate nothing in the data identifies, because the usual negative
control (pairs that never co-occur) is excluded from the candidate set by
construction. It is fixed a priori.

$p_1$ and $\nu$ maximise a zero-truncated beta-binomial likelihood over the
`r NPAIRS` species pairs recorded at one or more sites. Every site is a trial
for every pair, so $R_j$ = `r N_SITES` for all of them, and $n_j$ is the number
of sites that recorded the interaction. This is the SI's own estimate of $p_1$,
the proportion of networks in which the interaction is recorded (SI Section S9),
so $p_1$ covers the absent-partner step as well as realisation and detection:

$$
\ell(p_1, \nu) = \sum_j \log \frac{BB(n_j \mid R_j)}{1 - BB(0 \mid R_j)},
\qquad BB(n \mid R) = \frac{B(n+a,\; R-n+b)}{B(a,\,b)}
$$

with $a$ and $b$ as in the replicate factor. Dividing by $1 - BB(0 \mid R_j)$
corrects for having kept only pairs recorded at least once, which would otherwise
bias $p_1$ upward. The binomial coefficient is again left out: it does not
depend on $p_1$ or $\nu$, so it moves neither the fit nor the comparison below.
:::

**Open question.** `r N_CLIP` links
(`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * N_CLIP / nrow(obs))`) sit at the floor of the
prediction pipeline's sigmoid and carry no model information to calibrate.

## The four settings

|                                                       | uniform prior | degree-based prior |
|-------------------------------------------------------|---------------|--------------------|
| **A** model enters through the posterior as $\delta$   | A-uniform     | A-degree           |
| **B** calibrated model score enters as the prior       | B-uniform     | B-degree           |

Degree priors are global and replicate-based, so a link between two
well-connected species starts with more prior weight on the present-side
categories.

::: {.method}
**Methodological decisions.** Four settings rather than one, because the prior is
the most arguable choice in the whole construction. Showing that a conclusion
holds in all four is stronger than defending any single prior.

Each setting fixes two things in the posterior equation: the model switch $s$
and the three prior probabilities.

$s$ is the exponent on the model factor, $L_Y^{\,s}$. With $s = 1$ the factor
counts as usual, so the model enters as **evidence**. With $s = 0$ it becomes
$L_Y^{\,0} = 1$ for every category and drops out, so the model can enter through
the **prior** instead. Using both would count the model twice.

| Setting | $s$ | $\pi_Y$ | $\pi_l$ | $\pi_r$ |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| A-uniform | 1 | $\tfrac12$ | $\tfrac12$ | $\tfrac12$ |
| A-degree | 1 | $\tfrac12$ | $\pi_l^{\deg}$ | $\pi_r^{\deg}$ |
| B-uniform | 0 | $q_i$ | $\tfrac12$ | $\tfrac12$ |
| B-degree | 0 | $q_i$ | $\pi_l^{\deg}$ | $\pi_r^{\deg}$ |

$q_i$ is the Platt-calibrated score. The pipeline's `probability` column $p_i$
is inverted back to the raw score $x_i$, and a logistic regression of the local
record on that score, fitted on the other five sites, turns it into a
probability:

$$
x_i = \log\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}, \qquad q_i = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\alpha + \beta x_i)}}
$$

The degree prior is the configuration-model chance that two species connect,
given their degrees, then given five tries for the replicates:

$$
\pi_l^{\deg} = \min\!\left(\frac{d_{\text{pol}}\; d_{\text{pla}}}{L},\; 0.99\right),
\qquad \pi_r^{\deg} = 1 - \left(1 - \pi_l^{\deg}\right)^{5}
$$

$d_{\text{pol}}$ and $d_{\text{pla}}$ count the observed links of the pollinator
and the plant, and $L$ all observed links, each taken from the five non-focal
sites only, so the prior never sees the evidence it is combined with.
:::

**Open question.** A and B may be redundant for the camera test. Under a product
prior the posterior factorises into three independent parts, and the local part
does not depend on the model bit, so any test keyed to the local axis cannot
separate A from B. The camera results below bear this out exactly. Worth
deciding whether the manuscript presents four settings or two.

## A second axis: the likelihood

The four settings above vary the **prior**, and all of them assume links differ
in how readily a replicate site records them, governed by $\nu$. Each one
therefore gets a **twin** with that heterogeneity removed: A-uniform (no nu),
A-degree (no nu), and so on. Eight runs, four pairs.

Every prior needs its own twin rather than testing $\nu$ once. $\nu$ enters the
replicate factor for the four categories that claim the link is realisable
elsewhere, and the posterior is normalised, so how far a change there moves the
final probabilities depends on how much prior weight sat on those categories to
begin with. A uniform prior spreads that weight evenly; a degree prior
concentrates it on well-connected pairs. Testing $\nu$ under the uniform prior
alone would test it where it has the least room to matter, and the degree runs
are the ones carrying the within-category ranking.

::: {.method}
**Methodological decisions.** Removing heterogeneity means **removing** $\nu$,
not estimating it as infinite: the binomial is the beta-binomial at
$\nu \to \infty$. Under that constraint $p_1$ is the only free parameter left
and has to be **refitted**, because the mean of a beta-binomial is not the
binomial MLE. Here that matters: `r sprintf("%.3f", P1)` against
`r sprintf("%.3f", P1_HOM)` on the same `r NPAIRS` species pairs.

The twins are derived from the same list of priors in code rather than written
out again, so a change to a prior cannot reach one twin and miss the other.

In a twin, the replicate factor for $z_r = 1$ becomes a plain binomial,
$L_r = p_1^{\,n}(1-p_1)^{R-n}$, and $p_1$ is refitted with the same zero
truncation:

$$
\ell(p_1) = \sum_j \log \frac{p_1^{\,n_j}(1-p_1)^{R_j-n_j}}{1-(1-p_1)^{R_j}}
$$

The two models are nested, so which one the data prefer is a test rather than a
preference:

$$
LR = 2\,\bigl(\hat\ell_{\text{with }\nu} - \hat\ell_{\text{without }\nu}\bigr),
\qquad p = \tfrac12\, P\!\left(\chi^2_1 > LR\right),
\qquad \Delta AIC = 2 - LR
$$

$LR$ is twice the gain in fit from adding $\nu$. $p$ is the chance of a gain
that large if all links truly shared one rate; it is halved because "no
heterogeneity" is $\nu \to \infty$, the edge of its possible range. $\Delta AIC$
is AIC with $\nu$ minus AIC without, where AIC $= 2 \times$ (parameters)
$- \, 2\hat\ell$; negative means $\nu$ is worth its extra parameter.
:::

```{r het-lrt}
tibble(
  Model = c("beta-binomial (heterogeneous)", "binomial (no $\\nu$)"),
  `log-likelihood` = round(c(LL_BB, LL_B), 2),
  `$p_1$` = round(c(P1, P1_HOM), 3),
  `$\\nu$` = c(sprintf("%.2f", NU), "removed"),
  AIC = round(c(4 - 2*LL_BB, 2 - 2*LL_B), 1)
) %>% show()
```

The likelihood ratio is `r sprintf("%.2f", LR_NU)` on 1 df, boundary-corrected
$p$ = `r sprintf("%.3f", P_NU)`, so
**`r if (P_NU < 0.05) "the data support keeping $\\nu$" else "the data give no support for keeping $\\nu$"`**.
The twins show what that choice does to the results.

`r if (P1 * NU < 1) sprintf("**Open question.** $\\nu$ = %.2f sits outside the range the SI illustrates: it implies a beta shape parameter $a = p_1\\nu$ = %.2f, below 1. Widen the SI wording, or constrain the fit?", NU, P1 * NU) else ""`

# The starting point

The deterministic assignment at the richest site. Each cell is one candidate
link, coloured by its single assigned category.

```{r det-map}
include_graphics(file.path(FIG, "richest_site_map_obs_validated_with_rpi.png"))
```

This is the reference the posterior is compared against. It is complete and
unambiguous, and that is the problem: nothing in it separates a link the
evidence strongly supports from one that only just fell on that side of a
boundary.

**Takeaway.** The deterministic map is a reference, not a truth. Anything the
posterior does differently has to be judged against independent evidence, not
against this figure.

# Results

Categories appear in taxonomy order: the predicted classes first, then the
unpredicted class that dominates the candidate set.

In every map below, each cell is one link $i$ and **colour intensity is
$P(k \mid E_i)$** for the category $k$ the figure is about. A **black frame**
marks cells the deterministic rule assigned to $k$, and an **asterisk** marks a
link the cameras recorded. All four panels of a figure share one colour scale,
so shades are comparable between settings.

## Possibly missing

Predicted, recorded at other sites, not recorded here. The framework's
highest-priority category, and the one where the prescribed action is simply
more effort with the same method.

```{r fig-missing}
include_graphics(file.path(OUT, "panel_runs_missing.png"))
```

A-uniform is the counterpart of the deterministic assignment and B-uniform looks
much like it. The degree-based priors visibly change the picture.

```{r missing-agree}
post %>%
  filter(det_category == "possibly missing", run %in% RUNS) %>%
  group_by(run) %>%
  summarise(Links = n(),
            `Mean posterior on the assigned category` = round(mean(det_conf), 3),
            `Most likely category is the assigned one` =
              sprintf("%d%%", round(100 * mean(top_category == det_category))),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(match(run, RUNS)) %>%
  rename(Setting = run) %>% show()
```

::: {.method}
**Methodological decisions.** Frames come from the deterministic rule and are
identical in all four panels, so any difference between panels is the prior
talking and nothing else.

The table's two columns, over the $N$ links the hard rule assigned, with
$k^{\det}_i$ the category it gave link $i$:

$$
\text{mean posterior} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i P\!\left(k^{\det}_i \mid E_i\right),
\qquad
\text{agreement} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \mathbb{1}\!\left[\,\arg\max_k P(k \mid E_i) = k^{\det}_i\right]
$$

The first is how much probability each link puts on its assigned category; the
second is how often that category is also its most probable one.
:::

**Takeaway.** The label and the confidence are different quantities. A link can
sit in possibly missing under the hard rule while the posterior puts most of its
weight elsewhere. That is not a bug: the hard rule reads three bits as if they
were certain, and the posterior does not.


## Possibly forbidden

Neither predicted nor recorded anywhere: `r format(N_PF, big.mark = ",")` of
`r format(nrow(one), big.mark = ",")` links, by far the largest category.

```{r fig-forbidden}
include_graphics(file.path(OUT, "panel_runs_forbidden.png"))
```

**Takeaway.** Triage matters most here. A category holding well over half the
grid is unusable as a to-do list. The posterior orders it, and the cameras
corroborate that ordering, as shown two sections below.

**Discuss** Which model to use?

## Phantom

Predicted, but recorded nowhere. Genuinely ambiguous: either the model is wrong,
and an independent method finds nothing, or the interaction is invisible to the
method in use, and it does. The two readings predict opposite outcomes, which is
why the prescribed action is a different method rather than more effort.

```{r fig-phantom}
include_graphics(file.path(OUT, "panel_runs_phantom.png"))
```

**Takeaway.** Phantom is the one category with no predicted direction, so the
camera test below cannot confirm or refute it. The framework says as much
already, and the data does not contradict it.


## Where the posterior weight goes

```{r fig-dist}
include_graphics(file.path(OUT, "fig_category_distributions.png"))
```

Panel **a** is the expected number of links per category, panel **b** the spread
of per-link posteriors. The tick in panel a is the deterministic count, the same
in all four panels, so the gap between tick and bar is exactly what each prior
moves.

```{r run-table}
det_counts <- one %>% count(det_category, name = "det")
dev <- map_dfr(RUNS, function(rn) {
  s <- post %>% filter(run == rn)
  expct <- sapply(CATS, function(k) sum(s[[k]]))
  tibble(run = rn,
         abs_dev = sum(abs(expct[det_counts$det_category] - det_counts$det)))
})
post %>% filter(run %in% RUNS) %>% group_by(run) %>%
  summarise(sharp = round(mean(det_conf), 3),
            mode_ok = round(100 * mean(top_category == det_category)),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(dev, by = "run") %>%
  arrange(match(run, RUNS)) %>%
  transmute(Setting = run,
            `Mean posterior on the assigned label` = sharp,
            `Most likely category is the assigned one` = sprintf("%d%%", mode_ok),
            `Total gap from the deterministic counts` = round(abs_dev)) %>%
  show()
```

::: {.method}
**Methodological decisions.** Once a label becomes a distribution, the honest
headline number for a category is the **sum of its posterior column**, not a
count of links. Panel a plots the expected count, and the table's last column
compares it with the deterministic count $N_k^{\det}$:

$$
E[N_k] = \sum_i P(k \mid E_i),
\qquad
\text{total gap} = \sum_k \left|\, E[N_k] - N_k^{\det} \right|
$$

The dashed line in panel b is the ceiling on confidence for a link not recorded
locally, however many replicates record it:

$$
\kappa = \frac{(1-\epsilon_Y)(1-f)}{(1-f)+\epsilon_l} = `r sprintf("%.3f", KAPPA)`
$$

It holds only when every prior probability is $\tfrac12$, so it is drawn only in
the A-uniform panel; the other settings relax that condition and can exceed it.
:::

Two things are worth pausing on. A-uniform reproduces the deterministic label
most faithfully yet sits **farthest** from the deterministic counts, because it
holds the least weight on that label and so spreads the most. And the degree
settings are the **sharpest**, which is not the same as the most accurate.

**Takeaway.** Resembling the deterministic counts is not evidence of being
right, because those counts are not truth. The next section supplies a criterion
external to both.

Which of the two choices moves the posterior more, where the model enters or
the prior? Each row compares two settings that differ in one choice only.

```{r axis-compare}
key <- c("focal_site", "pollinator", "plant")
compare_runs <- function(r1, r2, changed) {
  a <- post %>% filter(run == r1) %>% arrange(across(all_of(key)))
  b <- post %>% filter(run == r2) %>% arrange(across(all_of(key)))
  d <- apply(abs(as.matrix(a[CATS]) - as.matrix(b[CATS])), 1, max)
  tibble(Changed = changed, Comparison = paste(r1, "vs", r2),
         gap  = sum(abs(colSums(a[CATS]) - colSums(b[CATS]))),
         mean_change = mean(d),
         same_top = mean(a$top_category == b$top_category))
}
axis_tbl <- bind_rows(
  compare_runs("A-uniform", "B-uniform", "where the model enters"),
  compare_runs("A-degree",  "B-degree",  "where the model enters"),
  compare_runs("A-uniform", "A-degree",  "prior"),
  compare_runs("B-uniform", "B-degree",  "prior"))
axis_tbl %>%
  transmute(Changed, Comparison,
            `Total gap in expected counts` = round(gap),
            `Mean change per link` = round(mean_change, 3),
            `Same most likely category` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * same_top)) %>%
  show()
by_model <- filter(axis_tbl, Changed != "prior")
by_prior <- filter(axis_tbl, Changed == "prior")
PRIOR_DOMINATES <- min(by_prior$gap) > max(by_model$gap) &&
  max(by_prior$same_top) < min(by_model$same_top)
```

The total gap is $\sum_k |E[N_k]_a - E[N_k]_b|$ between the two settings, and
the change per link is the largest shift in any one category,
$\max_k |P(k \mid E_i)_a - P(k \mid E_i)_b|$.

**Takeaway.** `r if (PRIOR_DOMINATES) "The settings differ mostly through the prior, not through where the model enters." else "Neither choice consistently dominates: compare the rows before choosing a setting."`
Moving the model from evidence to prior shifts at most
`r round(max(by_model$gap))` expected links and changes the most likely category
of at most `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * (1 - min(by_model$same_top)))` of links.
Adding the degree prior shifts at least `r round(min(by_prior$gap))` and changes
at least `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * (1 - max(by_prior$same_top)))`.

**B-degree is the only run in which the mean confidence in assignment is higher than 0.5 (might be an artifact how the model).**

## Where does each category's posterior go?

```{r leakage}
fl <- read_csv(file.path(OUT, "category_leakage_flows.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
sig <- tibble(category = CATS,
              zY = c(1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0),
              zl = c(1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0),
              zr = c(1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0))
moved <- fl %>%
  filter(from != to) %>%
  left_join(rename(sig, from = category, fY = zY, fl = zl, fr = zr), by = "from") %>%
  left_join(rename(sig, to = category), by = "to") %>%
  mutate(bits = (fY != zY) + (fl != zl) + (fr != zr))
kept <- fl %>% filter(from == to) %>% select(run, category = from, kept = share)

leak_run <- function(rn) {
  k <- filter(kept, run == rn); m <- filter(moved, run == rn)
  list(most   = k$category[which.max(k$kept)],   most_k  = max(k$kept),
       least  = k$category[which.min(k$kept)],   least_k = min(k$kept),
       pf_k   = k$kept[k$category == "possibly forbidden"],
       pf_rank = rank(-k$kept)[k$category == "possibly forbidden"],
       abs_top = m[which.max(m$w), ], rel_top = m[which.max(m$share), ],
       one_bit = sum(m$w[m$bits == 1]) / sum(m$w))
}
LK_U <- leak_run("B-uniform"); LK_D <- leak_run("B-degree")
flow_txt <- function(r) sprintf("%s \u2192 %s", r$from, r$to)
# is the largest absolute flow forbidden -> locally absent in both runs?
BIG_PF_LA <- all(c(flow_txt(LK_U$abs_top), flow_txt(LK_D$abs_top)) ==
                   "possibly forbidden \u2192 locally absent")
```

The distribution figure shows how many links each category ends up with. It
does not show where they came from. Here every arrow follows the posterior
from a deterministic category to another one, for all sites.

**Absolute weights.** Arrow width is the expected number of links moving.

```{r fig-leak-abs}
include_graphics(c(file.path(OUT, "fig_category_leakage_B_uniform.png"),
                   file.path(OUT, "fig_category_leakage_B_degree.png")))
```

**Relative weights.** Arrow width is the share of the source category's links
moving.

```{r fig-leak-rel}
include_graphics(c(file.path(OUT, "fig_category_leakage_B_uniform_relative.png"),
                   file.path(OUT, "fig_category_leakage_B_degree_relative.png")))
```

::: {.method}
**Methodological decisions.** For a deterministic category $k$ with
$N_k^{\det}$ links, the arrow to category $m$ carries

$$
F_{k \to m} = \sum_{i:\,k^{\det}_i = k} P(m \mid E_i),
\qquad
\text{share}_{k \to m} = \frac{F_{k \to m}}{N_k^{\det}}
$$

$F_{k \to k}$ is what the category keeps. A category's outgoing arrows plus
what it keeps add up to $N_k^{\det}$; its incoming arrows plus what it keeps
add up to $E[N_k]$. Both numbers are on each node's label, with the share kept.

*The two versions answer different questions.* The **absolute** version shows
where most of the expected links go. Large categories dominate it by size
alone. The **relative** version shows how stable each category is, whatever its
size: a category that keeps little of its mass has a hard label we should trust
less.

*Layout.* The taxonomy figure of the manuscript: columns are observed elsewhere
or not, rows are predicted then not predicted. A move to a neighbouring node
doubts one of the three bits; a diagonal move doubts two. Arrows take the
colour of the category they leave, node area is the deterministic count, and
each version uses one width scale for both runs.

*What moves is probability, not links.* No link switches category as a whole.
Each keeps part of its posterior and spreads the rest.
:::

**Takeaway.**

- In absolute numbers, the largest flow is
  `r flow_txt(LK_U$abs_top)` under B-uniform
  (`r round(LK_U$abs_top$w)` links) and `r flow_txt(LK_D$abs_top)` under
  B-degree (`r round(LK_D$abs_top$w)`). Possibly forbidden is the largest
  category, so it dominates this view.
- Relative to size, possibly forbidden keeps
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * LK_U$pf_k)` of its mass under B-uniform and
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * LK_D$pf_k)` under B-degree, where it ranks
  `r ifelse(LK_D$pf_rank == 1, "first", paste0(LK_D$pf_rank, " of 8"))` in
  stability. The least stable category is `r LK_U$least` under B-uniform
  (`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * LK_U$least_k)` kept) and `r LK_D$least` under
  B-degree (`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * LK_D$least_k)` kept).
- Most moving mass goes to a neighbouring category, doubting one bit:
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * LK_U$one_bit)` under B-uniform and
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * LK_D$one_bit)` under B-degree.
  `r if (BIG_PF_LA) sprintf("The biggest arrow in both runs, possibly forbidden → locally absent, crosses the replicate bit: with $p_1$ = %.2f, a link that can occur in the replicates still goes unrecorded at all %d of them more often than not (probability %.2f at the mean rate), so absence there is weak evidence.", P1, N_SITES - 1, (1 - P1)^(N_SITES - 1)) else ""`

## Does heterogeneity matter?

The same distribution figure for the four twins, in the same panel order, so it
reads directly against the one above. Each panel differs from its counterpart by
the **likelihood alone**: same prior, same model role, same rates, one carrying
heterogeneous $p_1$ and the other the single $p_1$ refitted without it. Anything
that moves between a panel and its counterpart is $\nu$, and nothing else.

```{r fig-het}
include_graphics(file.path(OUT, "fig_category_distributions_no_nu.png"))
```

Expected links gained or lost per category when $\nu$ is removed, within each
prior:

$$
\Delta E[N_k] = E[N_k]_{\text{without }\nu} - E[N_k]_{\text{with }\nu}
$$

Paired by prior, because the question is what $\nu$ does inside a prior, not
which prior sits closest to the deterministic counts.

```{r het-shift}
expected_by <- function(rn) sapply(CATS, function(k) sum(post[[k]][post$run == rn]))
shift_tbl <- tibble(Category = CATS) %>%
  bind_cols(as_tibble(setNames(
    lapply(RUNS, function(rn) expected_by(paste0(rn, " (no nu)")) - expected_by(rn)),
    RUNS))) %>%
  left_join(post %>% filter(run == "A-uniform") %>%
              count(Category = det_category, name = "Deterministic"),
            by = "Category") %>%
  relocate(Deterministic, .after = Category) %>%
  arrange(desc(Deterministic)) %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(RUNS), ~round(.x, 1)))
show(shift_tbl)
```

The largest single shift is
`r round(max(abs(as.matrix(shift_tbl[RUNS]))), 1)` links out of
`r format(nrow(one), big.mark = ",")`. $\kappa$ does not change at all, because
$\nu$ does not appear in it.

```{r het-direction}
# net expected links moved into the four "not realisable" categories, per prior,
# from unrounded values so a small shift keeps its sign
ZR0 <- c("locally unique", "phantom", "weakly-supported", "possibly forbidden")
to_zr0 <- sapply(RUNS, function(rn)
  sum(expected_by(paste0(rn, " (no nu)"))[ZR0] - expected_by(rn)[ZR0]))
HET_DIRECTION <- if (all(to_zr0 > 0)) {
  'from "realisable in the replicates" toward "not realisable"'
} else if (all(to_zr0 < 0)) {
  'from "not realisable" toward "realisable in the replicates"'
} else {
  "in different directions under different priors"
}
```

The shifts come in equal and opposite pairs. Each category that says
"realisable in the replicates" ($z_r = 1$) loses exactly what its partner saying
"not realisable" ($z_r = 0$) gains: recurrent and locally unique, possibly
missing and phantom, model-elusive and weakly-supported, locally absent and
possibly forbidden. $\nu$ acts only through the replicate factor, so it can
move probability only across $z_r$. Here the movement runs `r HET_DIRECTION`.

Totals can hide movement at the level of single links, so the same comparison
link by link, with $\Delta_i = \max_k \left| P(k \mid E_i)_{\text{without }\nu} - P(k \mid E_i)_{\text{with }\nu} \right|$:

```{r het-links}
key <- c("focal_site", "pollinator", "plant")
het_links <- map_dfr(RUNS, function(rn) {
  a <- post %>% filter(run == rn) %>% arrange(across(all_of(key)))
  b <- post %>% filter(run == paste0(rn, " (no nu)")) %>% arrange(across(all_of(key)))
  d <- apply(abs(as.matrix(a[CATS]) - as.matrix(b[CATS])), 1, max)
  rho <- sapply(c("possibly missing", "phantom", "possibly forbidden"), function(k) {
    i <- a$det_category == k
    cor(a[[k]][i], b[[k]][i], method = "spearman")
  })
  tibble(Setting = rn,
         `Mean change per link` = mean(d),
         `Largest change` = max(d),
         `Links moving more than 0.05` = sum(d > 0.05),
         same_top = mean(a$top_category == b$top_category),
         min_rho = min(rho))
})
het_links %>%
  transmute(Setting,
            `Mean change per link` = round(`Mean change per link`, 3),
            `Largest change` = round(`Largest change`, 2),
            `Links moving more than 0.05`,
            `Same most likely category` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * same_top),
            `Within-category rank correlation, lowest` = round(min_rho, 3)) %>%
  show()
```

The last column is the Spearman correlation between the two posteriors across
each category's own links, taken for possibly missing, phantom and possibly
forbidden, and reporting the lowest of the three. 1 means removing $\nu$ leaves
the ranking untouched.

The three category maps for the twins are below, one per corroboration action,
each mirroring the four-run figure of the same category above.

```{r fig-het-maps}
include_graphics(c(file.path(OUT, "panel_runs_missing_no_nu.png"),
                   file.path(OUT, "panel_runs_phantom_no_nu.png"),
                   file.path(OUT, "panel_runs_forbidden_no_nu.png")))
```

Each figure carries its own shared colour scale, so compare **shapes** between a
figure and its counterpart above, and shades only within one figure.

**Takeaway.** Removing $\nu$ moves at most
`r round(max(abs(as.matrix(shift_tbl[RUNS]))))` expected links, `r HET_DIRECTION`.
The share of links whose most likely category changes is
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * (1 - min(het_links$same_top[grepl("uniform", het_links$Setting)])))`
at most under the uniform priors and
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * (1 - min(het_links$same_top[grepl("degree", het_links$Setting)])))`
at most under the degree priors, so the priors do respond differently. Within-category rankings stay
nearly identical (lowest Spearman `r sprintf("%.2f", min(het_links$min_rho))`),
and `r sum(camsum$no_nu == sprintf("%d/%d same", length(RUNS), length(RUNS)))`
of the `r nrow(camsum)` camera calls are unchanged under every prior.
`r if (P_NU < 0.05) "The data support keeping $\\nu$" else "The data give no support for keeping $\\nu$"`
(boundary $p$ = `r sprintf("%.3f", P_NU)`).

## Does confidence buy anything?

The question the whole exercise turns on: if we chase the links the posterior is
confident about, do we find more? For possibly forbidden the prediction runs the
other way, so the test is whether cameras find **fewer** records among links with
a high forbidden posterior.

::: {.method}
**Methodological decisions.** This is the measurement to scrutinise, so it is
worth being explicit about each choice.

*Independent evidence.* Cameras ran in parallel with direct observation and the
posterior never saw them, so they are a fourth source of evidence rather than a
restatement of the three the posterior uses.

*Who is in the test.* A link is inside the **camera grid** when both partners
appear in that site's camera data. A zero then means the cameras saw both
species there but never together, which is a real negative. Links outside the
grid are dropped, since they can neither confirm nor refute.

*How agreement is measured.* One logistic regression per category per setting,
predicting whether the cameras recorded a link from that category's posterior.
The effect is reported as an odds ratio per one standard deviation of the
posterior, so categories with different spreads stay comparable.

*The adjustment that makes it a real test.* The direct observation is held
fixed. Categories are defined partly by that observation, so without this the
posterior would largely be re-describing it. Holding it fixed asks: among links
whose direct observation was the same, does the posterior still say which ones
the cameras find? A second model also adjusts for site, since camera coverage
differs between sites.

*The model.* For category $k$, over the links inside the camera grid, with
$c_i = 1$ when the cameras recorded link $i$:

$$
\log\frac{P(c_i = 1)}{1 - P(c_i = 1)} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 z_i + \beta_2 O_{l,i},
\qquad
z_i = \frac{P(k \mid E_i) - \overline{P}}{\operatorname{sd}(P)}
$$

$z_i$ is the posterior standardised to mean 0 and standard deviation 1, and the
site-adjusted version adds one term per site. The table reports

$$
OR = e^{\beta_1}
$$

the factor by which the **odds** of a camera record change for one standard
deviation more posterior. Above 1, higher posterior goes with more records.

*The probability column.* An odds ratio is not a change in probability, so the
same fit is translated back. Every link is predicted twice, at the average
posterior ($z = 0$) and one standard deviation above it ($z = 1$), keeping its
own $O_l$, and the predictions are averaged:

$$
\bar p_0 = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \sigma\!\left(\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_2 O_{l,i}\right),
\qquad
\bar p_1 = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \sigma\!\left(\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 + \hat\beta_2 O_{l,i}\right),
\qquad
\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}
$$

The table shows $\bar p_0 \to \bar p_1$ in percent, ranged over the settings
where the effect is significant.

*The verdict.* A setting supports a category when $p < 0.05$ for $\beta_1$ and
$OR$ falls on the side the category claims: above 1 for "higher", below 1 for
"lower".

*The expected direction* is set from what each category **claims
ecologically**, not from its observation bit. These differ. Possibly missing
carries "not seen here", yet its whole claim is that the interaction is present
and was missed, so cameras should find it *more* often.
:::

```{r cam-table}
run_cols <- RUNS[RUNS %in% names(camsum)]
all_sig <- camsum %>% select(all_of(run_cols)) %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ str_detect(.x, fixed("*")))) %>%
  rowSums() == length(run_cols)

camsum %>%
  rename(Category = category, Expect = expect,
         `Camera-confirmed` = confirmed, `%` = pct_conf,
         Verdict = verdict, `Site-adjusted` = site,
         `Camera chance, mean -> +1 SD` = chance) %>%
  show() %>%
  row_spec(which(all_sig), bold = TRUE)
```

Rows in **bold** are the four categories where the effect is significant in all
four prior settings.

Reading the table: the setting columns are odds ratios per one standard
deviation of that category's posterior, with the direct observation held fixed.
Above 1, a higher posterior goes with more camera records. Stars are `***`
$p<0.001$, `**` $p<0.01$, `*` $p<0.05$. The last column translates the same
effect onto the probability scale, which is the figure to quote in prose.

The `no_nu` column is the heterogeneity check. Eight odds-ratio columns would be
unreadable, and the question the twins answer is narrow: does removing $\nu$
change the **call**? A call is "significant and upward", "significant and
downward", or "no signal", which is what the verdict is built from. Each twin is
compared with its own prior, so `4/4 same` means $\nu$ changes nothing for that
category under any of the four priors.

`n` counts links of that category **inside the camera grid**, not the whole
category: possibly forbidden has `r format(N_PF, big.mark = ",")` links in total
and `r camsum$n[camsum$category == "possibly forbidden"]` here.

`r N_SUPPORTED` categories are supported in all `r length(RUNS)` settings, and
`r N_SUPPORTED_SITE` of those `r N_SUPPORTED` still hold after the site
adjustment:

- **recurrent** and **possibly missing** go the right way upward. Possibly
  missing is the one that matters, because its claim is that the interaction is
  present and direct observation missed it.
- **weakly-supported** and **possibly forbidden** go the right way downward. For
  possibly forbidden, one standard deviation up the posterior takes the chance
  of a camera record from
  `r sub(" -> ", "% to ", camsum$chance[camsum$category == "possibly forbidden"])`%,
  ranged over the settings.

**Takeaway.** The posterior is not merely re-describing the observations.
Holding the direct observation fixed, it still orders links by how likely an
independent method is to find them, in the direction each category claims. That
is the operational value of the confidence layer: it turns a category into a
ranked list, which is what makes a category of
`r format(N_PF, big.mark = ",")` possibly-forbidden links actionable at all.

**Open questions.**

- **Locally absent contradicts its expected direction** in the two degree
  settings. Its claim is that the link is feasible in the system but not
  realised here, so cameras should find it less often, and under degree priors
  they find it more. This needs an explanation before it reaches the manuscript.
- $\epsilon_l$ is fitted on the same camera records this test uses. Holding the
  direct observation fixed limits the exposure, since $\epsilon_l$ enters
  through the local axis, but a leave-one-site-out refit would remove what
  remains.

## Where to look, species by species

```{r per-plant}
pp <- read_csv(file.path(OUT, "per_plant_expected_counts.csv"),
               show_col_types = FALSE)
SITE   <- unique(pp$focal_site)
N_CAND <- unique(pp$candidates)
N_PLANTS <- n_distinct(pp$plant)

# winner-takes-all: how many links have a category as their single most likely
site_post <- post %>% filter(focal_site == SITE, run == "B-uniform")
PM_TOP <- sum(site_post$top_category == "possibly missing")
PM_EXP <- sum(site_post$`possibly missing`)

# possibly missing per plant, per run
pm <- pp %>% filter(category == "possibly missing") %>%
  group_by(run) %>%
  summarise(lo = min(expected), hi = max(expected),
            top = plant[which.max(expected)],
            top_e = max(expected), top_sd = sd[which.max(expected)],
            .groups = "drop")
pm_u <- filter(pm, run == "B-uniform"); pm_d <- filter(pm, run == "B-degree")

# plant x category cells where the deterministic count falls outside +/- 1 SD
outside <- pp %>% group_by(run) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(abs(deterministic - expected) > sd), total = n(),
            .groups = "drop")

# the degree prior: species recorded at one site only
links_obs <- obs %>% filter(ground_truth == 1)
one_site <- function(col) links_obs %>% distinct(.data[[col]], focal_site) %>%
  count(.data[[col]]) %>% summarise(one = sum(n == 1), all = n())
PLA1 <- one_site("lower_level"); POL1 <- one_site("higher_level")
REALISED <- c("recurrent", "locally unique", "model-elusive", "weakly-supported")
zero_real <- pp %>% filter(run == "B-degree", category %in% REALISED) %>%
  group_by(plant) %>%
  summarise(exp = sum(expected), det = sum(deterministic), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(exp < 0.05, det > 0)
```

Field effort is often planned per species: a camera or an extra observation
round goes to a plant. Two steps: first all plants at `r SITE` side by side,
then one plant at a time.

### Step 1: all plants, category by category

For each of the `r N_PLANTS` plants, how many of its `r N_CAND` candidate links
the posterior places in each category.

```{r fig-per-plant-uniform}
include_graphics(file.path(OUT, "fig_per_plant_B_uniform.png"))
```

```{r fig-per-plant-degree}
include_graphics(file.path(OUT, "fig_per_plant_B_degree.png"))
```

Each dot is the expected number of the plant's links in that category, the
whisker $\pm 1$ SD (cut at zero), and the tick the deterministic count. Plants
are ordered by degree, highest at the bottom, as in the maps. Every panel has
its own axis, because possibly forbidden runs to tens of links and possibly
missing to a few.

The same posteriors as each plant's composition: a cell is the plant's average
posterior for that category, so every row sums to 1 and a row shows where that
plant's mass goes.

```{r fig-share-uniform}
include_graphics(file.path(OUT, "fig_per_plant_share_B_uniform.png"))
```

```{r fig-share-degree}
include_graphics(file.path(OUT, "fig_per_plant_share_B_degree.png"))
```

```{r daucus-me}
dc <- post %>% filter(focal_site == SITE, plant == "Daucus carota", run == "B-degree")
DC_OBS_PRED <- sum(dc$O_l == 1 & dc$Y == 1)
DC_ME <- pp %>% filter(plant == "Daucus carota", category == "model-elusive")
# under B the split recovers q exactly: q = P(rec) / (P(rec) + P(model-elusive))
dc_q <- dc %>% filter(O_l == 1, Y == 1, recurrent + `model-elusive` > 1e-9) %>%
  mutate(q = recurrent / (recurrent + `model-elusive`))
DC_WEAK <- sum(dc_q$q < 0.6)
```

**Observation.** Model-elusive mass on a plant does not mean its links went
unpredicted. *Daucus carota* has no model-elusive links in the deterministic
assignment, yet an average posterior of
`r sprintf("%.2f", DC_ME$share[DC_ME$run == "B-degree"])` under B-degree. It
comes from its `r DC_OBS_PRED` observed links, all of which the model predicted.
Model-elusive and recurrent differ only in the model bit, so the posterior
splits a realised link between them by how far it trusts the model's call:
$1 - q_i$ under B. `r DC_WEAK` of them have a calibrated score below 0.6, so
the mass flags weak model calls, not new ecology.

::: {.method}
**Methodological decisions.**

*What is summed.* For plant $j$, over its candidate links $i \in j$:

$$
E[N_{kj}] = \sum_{i \in j} P(k \mid E_i),
\qquad
\operatorname{SD}(N_{kj}) = \sqrt{\sum_{i \in j} P(k \mid E_i)\,\bigl(1 - P(k \mid E_i)\bigr)}
$$

A link's eight posteriors sum to 1, so a plant's eight expected counts sum to
its number of candidate links, `r N_CAND` here, not to 1.

*Why the sum and not the average.* The average posterior, the sum divided by
the number of candidates, is also a valid summary: it is the **share** of the
plant's candidate links in each category, and its eight values add up to 1. We
use the sum for three reasons.

```{r share-example}
cand_by_site <- post %>% filter(run == "B-uniform") %>%
  group_by(focal_site) %>% summarise(cand = n_distinct(pollinator))
SMALL <- cand_by_site %>% slice_min(cand, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
N_POL_CAND <- post %>% filter(run == "B-uniform", focal_site == SITE) %>%
  pull(plant) %>% n_distinct()
```

1. **Effort is planned in links, not in shares.** The field question is how
   many links a plant holds that still need corroboration. The sum answers it
   directly; the share has to be multiplied back by the number of candidates.
2. **A share means different amounts in different places.** A share of 0.10 is
   `r sprintf("%.1f", 0.10 * N_CAND)` links for a plant at `r SITE`
   (`r N_CAND` candidates), `r sprintf("%.1f", 0.10 * SMALL$cand)` at
   `r SMALL$focal_site` (`r SMALL$cand` candidates), and
   `r sprintf("%.1f", 0.10 * N_POL_CAND)` for a pollinator at `r SITE`
   (`r N_POL_CAND` candidates). Sums stay comparable across sites and between
   plants and pollinators; shares do not.
3. **The SD is in the same units as the answer.** The SD of the sum is in links.
   The SD of a share shrinks as candidates grow, so it looks more certain for a
   species with many candidates without saying anything about how many links
   are at stake.

Within this one site every plant has the same `r N_CAND` candidates, so the two
rank plants identically, and the choice only matters once plants are compared
with other sites or with pollinators.

One more alternative was set aside:

- **Counting each link's most likely category** is winner takes all. A
  category that is rarely any link's first choice counts as zero even when it
  holds real probability across many links: under B-uniform at this site,
  `r PM_TOP` links have possibly missing as their most likely category, against
  `r sprintf("%.1f", PM_EXP)` expected. It repeats the problem of hard labels.

The single most probable count was also considered. It always lies within one
of the sum (Darroch 1964), so it adds nothing, and unlike the sums the eight do
not add up to the candidates.

*The heatmap uses the average.* With $n_j$ the plant's candidate links,

$$
\bar P_{kj} = \frac{E[N_{kj}]}{n_j} = \frac{1}{n_j}\sum_{i \in j} P(k \mid E_i),
\qquad \sum_k \bar P_{kj} = 1
$$

Here the question is a plant's composition, read across a row, and a share is
its natural scale. At this site every $n_j$ is `r N_CAND`, so the heatmap and
the counts above carry the same information. Each column runs from white to its
category's colour in the map key, on one intensity scale for all cells: full
colour is the highest average posterior in that figure. Values are printed
because small shares are hard to tell apart by shade, and the palest category
colours never get dark.

*What the SD shows.* How far the true count could plausibly sit from the
expected one. Two limits: it treats a plant's links as independent, but links
sharing a plant also share its sampling effort (SI Section S7), so the real
spread is wider; and at small counts the spread is skewed, so the whisker is
cut at zero rather than read as symmetric.

*Which runs.* B-uniform and B-degree. Both carry the calibrated score, and the
prior is the choice that moves the posterior (takeaway under "Where the
posterior weight goes"). Heterogeneity is kept, since removing it changes little
(takeaway under "Does heterogeneity matter?").
:::

**Takeaway.** Summed per plant, the posterior turns categories into an effort
plan with its uncertainty attached. For possibly missing, the category that
calls for more of the same method, expected counts run from
`r sprintf("%.1f", pm_u$lo)` to `r sprintf("%.1f", pm_u$hi)` per plant under
B-uniform and from `r sprintf("%.1f", pm_d$lo)` to `r sprintf("%.1f", pm_d$hi)`
under B-degree, led by *`r pm_u$top`*
(`r sprintf("%.1f ± %.1f", pm_u$top_e, pm_u$top_sd)`) and
*`r pm_d$top`* (`r sprintf("%.1f ± %.1f", pm_d$top_e, pm_d$top_sd)`)
respectively. `r if (pm_d$hi - pm_d$lo > pm_u$hi - pm_u$lo) "The degree prior separates plants more." else "The uniform prior separates plants at least as well."`
The deterministic count falls outside $\pm 1$ SD in
`r outside$n[outside$run == "B-uniform"]` of `r outside$total[1]` plant–category
cells under B-uniform and `r outside$n[outside$run == "B-degree"]` under
B-degree: the cells where the posterior and the hard labels disagree most about
a plant.

### Step 2: one plant, where its posterior mass goes

Step 1 compares plants within a category. Step 2 turns this around: for one
plant, it compares its eight categories with each other, to see where that
plant's posterior mass goes. Shown for *`r NOTE_PLANTS[1]`* and
*`r NOTE_PLANTS[2]`*; the script draws any plant listed in `FOCAL_PLANTS`.

```{r fig-plant-1}
include_graphics(c(plant_fig(NOTE_PLANTS[1], "B-uniform"),
                   plant_fig(NOTE_PLANTS[1], "B-degree")))
```

```{r fig-plant-2}
include_graphics(c(plant_fig(NOTE_PLANTS[2], "B-uniform"),
                   plant_fig(NOTE_PLANTS[2], "B-degree")))
```

::: {.method}
**Methodological decisions.** The values are the step-1 expected counts and SDs
for that plant, with the same formulas, so the eight rows add up to its
`r N_CAND` candidate links. Dot, whisker and tick mean what they mean in step 1.

*One axis for all eight rows*, unlike step 1, because the comparison is now
between categories of the same plant. *The same axis in both runs' figures*, so
the two can be read against each other directly.
:::

```{r plant-takeaway}
plant_summary <- pp %>%
  filter(plant %in% NOTE_PLANTS) %>%
  group_by(plant, run) %>%
  summarise(top = category[which.max(expected)],
            top_e = max(expected),
            top_share = max(expected) / first(candidates),
            n_out = sum(abs(deterministic - expected) > sd),
            .groups = "drop")
plant_line <- function(pl) {
  s <- plant_summary %>% filter(plant == pl)
  u <- filter(s, run == "B-uniform"); d <- filter(s, run == "B-degree")
  sprintf("*%s*: most mass in %s under B-uniform (%.1f links, %.0f%%) and in %s under B-degree (%.1f links, %.0f%%); the deterministic count falls outside $\\pm 1$ SD in %d and %d of the eight categories.",
          pl, u$top, u$top_e, 100 * u$top_share,
          d$top, d$top_e, 100 * d$top_share, u$n_out, d$n_out)
}
```

**Takeaway.** Per plant, the posterior shows which categories hold its mass and
how far that departs from the hard labels.

- `r plant_line(NOTE_PLANTS[1])`
- `r plant_line(NOTE_PLANTS[2])`

**Open question: the degree prior. `r PLA1$one` of `r PLA1$all` plants and
`r POL1$one` of `r POL1$all` pollinators are recorded at a single site. Their
degree in the replicates is 0, so $\pi_l^{\deg} = \pi_r^{\deg} = 0$ and their
locally observed links are forced into categories not realised here:
`r if (nrow(zero_real)) paste0("under B-degree, *", paste(zero_real$plant, collapse = "* and *"), "* get no expected links realised here despite ", sum(zero_real$det), " observed") else "no plant at this site is affected"`.
The degree prior also draws on the same five sites as the replicate evidence
$n$, a partial double count. One fix to weigh: degrees from all six sites,
leaving out the pair's own records.**


## How much is replication worth here?

```{r fig-accum}
include_graphics(file.path(OUT, "fig_accumulation_empirical.png"))
```

Figure 3a of the manuscript, driven by the rates fitted here rather than
illustrative ones. Solid within the six-site design, dashed for hypothetical
extra sites.

::: {.method}
**Methodological decisions.** The curve comes from the same posterior function
as everything above, under A-uniform, swept over the number of replicates, so
this figure and the analysis cannot drift apart. The evidence is the
possibly-missing signature, predicted, not seen here, and detected in every
replicate that could have found it:

$$
E = \left(\hat Y = 1,\;\; O_l = 0,\;\; n = R\right), \qquad R = 0, 1, 2, \ldots
$$

Each coloured line is $P(k \mid E)$ for one category. The teal line is
**feasibility confidence**, the probability that the link is realised here or
realisable elsewhere, whichever category it falls in:

$$
\varphi = 1 - P(\text{phantom} \mid E) - P(\text{possibly forbidden} \mid E)
$$

The dashed horizontal line is $\kappa$, defined under the posterior weight
figure above.
:::

How fast the curve climbs is set by how far $p_1$ = `r sprintf("%.2f", P1)`
sits above $f$ = `r sprintf("%.2f", F_POS)`: the wider that gap, the more each
recording replicate is worth. The level it climbs toward is $\kappa$, which does
not involve $p_1$ at all.

**Takeaway.** A few replicates exhaust what replication can buy here.
$\kappa$ = `r sprintf("%.3f", KAPPA)` follows from the error rates by algebra: it
is a structural ceiling, not a measurement, and no amount of sampling passes it.
The way past it is a better model or a better local method, which is exactly the
corroboration action the framework already prescribes for the categories sitting
against it. That is an argument for the framework, not a limitation of it.

## Conclusions
```{r conclusions}
# expected links per category over every site, for the four prior settings
exp_all <- function(rn, k) sum(post[[k]][post$run == rn])

# plants with deterministic model-elusive links whose average posterior matches Daucus
me_b <- pp %>% filter(run == "B-degree", category == "model-elusive")
DC_SHARE <- me_b$share[me_b$plant == "Daucus carota"]
me_peers <- me_b %>%
  filter(plant != "Daucus carota", deterministic > 0,
         round(share, 2) == round(DC_SHARE, 2))

# possibly missing: the deterministic leader, the B-degree ranking, and plants
# with none assigned that the uniform prior expects at least one of
pm_all <- pp %>% filter(category == "possibly missing")
PM_DET_TOP <- pm_all %>% filter(run == "B-degree") %>%
  slice_max(deterministic, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>% pull(plant)
PM_DEG_TOP3 <- pm_all %>% filter(run == "B-degree") %>%
  arrange(desc(expected)) %>% slice_head(n = 3) %>% pull(plant)
PM_UNI_NEW <- pm_all %>%
  filter(run == "B-uniform", deterministic == 0, expected >= 1) %>% nrow()
PM_ZERO <- pm_all %>% filter(run == "B-uniform", deterministic == 0) %>% nrow()
it <- function(x) paste0("*", x, "*")
```

::: {.conclusion}
**Conclusions**

1. The posterior allows us to add confidence and uncertainty to the
   deterministic assignment, and by doing so to focus our efforts more
   effectively (*Does confidence buy anything?*).
2. The degree prior preserves the general trends seen with the uniform prior,
   but more of the posterior goes to possibly forbidden
   (`r format(round(exp_all("B-degree", "possibly forbidden")), big.mark = ",")`
   expected links against
   `r round(exp_all("B-uniform", "possibly forbidden"))` under B-uniform, all
   sites), and locally unique and weakly-supported become much less likely
   (`r round(exp_all("B-uniform", "locally unique"))` →
   `r round(exp_all("B-degree", "locally unique"))` and
   `r round(exp_all("B-uniform", "weakly-supported"))` →
   `r round(exp_all("B-degree", "weakly-supported"))`).
3. The heatmaps give an overview per species and can help decide on the action
   when uncertainty is considered. For example, *Daucus carota* is not assigned
   any model-elusive links deterministically, yet when we consider $\pi_Y$ its
   average model-elusive posterior is `r sprintf("%.2f", DC_SHARE)` under
   B-degree`r if (nrow(me_peers)) paste0(", as high as ", paste(it(me_peers$plant), collapse = " and "), ", which do have model-elusive links deterministically") else ""`.
   This is because we doubt the model's call, so some links that were
   recurrent or locally unique may be poorly predicted. If this is an
   important focal species, model revision might be considered.
4. When we look at the distributions, we can see the SD that follows from the
   confidence we added to the deterministic calls, and the leakage between
   categories. Species can then rank differently. Deterministically,
   `r it(PM_DET_TOP)` has the most possibly missing links, but under B-degree
   the leading plant is `r it(PM_DEG_TOP3[1])`, then `r it(PM_DEG_TOP3[2])` and
   `r it(PM_DEG_TOP3[3])`. Even under the uniform prior,
   `r if (PM_UNI_NEW == PM_ZERO) paste("all", PM_ZERO) else paste(PM_UNI_NEW, "of the", PM_ZERO)`
   plants with no possibly missing links are now expected to have at least
   one.
5. Considering degree as the prior, in its current form, biases the results,
   especially when examining the species level (open question above).
6. When we add uncertainty, a lot of possibly forbidden links move to other
   categories, but this is mostly because it is the largest category. Relative
   to its size, it keeps `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * LK_D$pf_k)` of its links
   under B-degree, and other categories leak much more (e.g., `r LK_D$least`
   keeps only `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * LK_D$least_k)`).
7. Most links move to a neighbouring category, so the posterior usually doubts
   one piece of evidence at a time.`r if (BIG_PF_LA) " The biggest move, from possibly forbidden to locally absent, happens because not seeing a link in the replicates is weak evidence when detection there is low." else ""`
:::
